title: Charlemagne (800)
hookLine: crowned in Rome on Christmas Day; schools and a mixed legacy

cards: Christmas, in Saint Peter's in Rome. The king of the Franks has come to Mass: tall, his biographer tells us, and usually dressed plainly, in the clothes of his own people.
As he rises from prayer, the pope places a crown on his head, and the crowd acclaims him as emperor. His biographer, Einhard, adds something odd.
Charles said afterward that if he'd known what the pope intended, he wouldn't have gone into the church that day, feast or no feast. Today, Charlemagne.

teach.b: Nobody is sure what Charles meant. Some readers think he didn't want the pope deciding who was emperor; others think it was modesty for show. Einhard doesn't explain.
Take the cathedrals side first. Charles cared about learning. He gathered scholars at his court, among them Alcuin, a teacher from York.
He wanted priests who could read, schools attached to monasteries and cathedrals, and books copied clearly.
Einhard says Charles himself tried to learn to write late in life, keeping tablets under his pillow, but began too late to get far. Now the crowns side. Charles was also a conqueror.
Einhard describes long wars against the Saxons, who were made to give up their old worship and accept baptism as a condition of peace.

Even in his own court, voices pushed back: Alcuin wrote that faith comes from the will and can't be forced, that a person can be drawn to faith but not compelled into it. So which is he, a builder or a conqueror?
Honestly, both. Einhard records the schools and the books, and he records the Saxons too.

That closes a week of people who carried the faith in very different ways: Isidore gathering all knowledge, Bede finishing, Boniface's oak falling, John of Damascus's window, the monks on Mount Athos, two brothers teaching in their own tongue, and today a crown, with a cathedral school beside it.

how: Charlemagne is not a saint on the Church's universal calendar; his schools and the books copied in his time are studied as part of how the Church kept learning alive.

games.q: you're Alcuin, a teacher at the king's court. the king is forcing conquered people into baptism. what do you do?
o: stay quiet; it's not your place.
write that faith comes from the will and can't be forced.
games.why: Alcuin wrote that a person can be drawn to faith but not compelled into it, a voice of conscience inside the court.

practice: Bring to mind one small place where you have power over someone: a child, a team at work, a younger sibling, even a pet.
Ask slowly where you've used that power to build something good, like a school, and where you've used it to push someone into your way of doing things, and look at both without judgment.
If you pray, ask God for the grace to draw people, never to force them.

wordCard.voice: Charlemagne. Charles the Great, king of the Franks, crowned emperor in Rome at Christmas: a builder of schools, and a conqueror. Today's word.
